project-description.description:
This project rethinks the role of media in times of violence and political transition. Rather than documenting atrocities directly, GPS-Archives engages audiences of state-sponsored, ‘apolitical,’ and ‘entertaining’ media—soap operas, songs, TV shows, and radio programs—to establish a public archive of life under Syria’s dictatorship (1971–2024). By reclaiming media once consumed under repression, the project turns them into entry points for narrating experiences of detention, torture, disappearance, and massacre. Victims, survivors, and their families reactivate these repertoires as mnemonic prompts that shape justice narratives from below.
Whether locally produced or globally circulated, these glocal repertoires need not be overtly ‘activist’ to matter. Their meanings exceed their original contexts, persisting as shared references that both reveal and are reshaped by atrocity. In a society fragmented along geographic, ethnic, and sectarian lines before and after the fall of the Assad regime, GPS-Archives explores how memory work can advance mutual care and trust through collective archiving among Syrians within and beyond the country. It also enables diasporic communities to share fuller accounts of their lives with host-country publics, reclaiming narrative authority and situating violence within everyday transnational worlds.
Through ethnographic fieldwork across Syria, Egypt, and Germany—combining archiving workshops, narrative interviews, and co-annotation of circulating and private media collections—the project develops a participatory model grounded in practices of watching and listening. Alongside academic outputs, a community-archive hybrid platform that features digital and on-site exhibitions co-curated with interlocutors models new ways of sharing memories of violence. By centering lived engagements with popular media, GPS-Archives creates a vernacular pathway for Syrians to reclaim and preserve ownership of their experiences in times of transformation.

items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper examines the way Cuba was represented in noticeable online media in connection with Bernie Sanders’ aspirations to become the Democratic nominee for the 2020 presidential election. Traditional anticommunism and a historical one-sided view on Cuba in the press, as well as widespread conceptual confusion about “socialism” in US society, converged against Sanders over the run-up to the nomination, especially at a crucial moment in February 2020 when he was the frontrunner and was interviewed by CBS. The paper analyses the reaction of the online press to Sanders’ comments on Cuba during the interview, but also considers other US press reports during 2019 as well as specialised literature on the topic. Discourse Analysis parameters are brought forward to highlight ideological discourse representations in the media.</jats:p>
